### Why a single hillshade can look *harsh*
A hillshade layer is a **raw illumination of the DEM** – every pixel is lit from a single sun direction, with a fixed contrast.  
If the sun is set to a low angle, the shadows become deep black and the highlights stay bright, which makes the layer look “hard” or “crisp”.  
The default style (`hillshade-method: "standard"`) does not smooth the result, so the effect is especially noticeable on low‑resolution DEM tiles or on steep terrain.

Below are the most common levers you can turn to turn that harshness into a softer, more map‑friendly relief.

---

## 1. Choose a softer hillshade algorithm

MapLibre ships with a handful of built‑in shading methods. The newer ones are designed to look more natural without having to stack several layers.

| Method | What it does | Typical visual impact |
|--------|--------------|-----------------------|
| **`standard`** (default) | Classic single‑light source, raster‑based | High contrast, harsh shadows |
| **`basic`** | Faster, lower‑resolution lighting | Slightly softer, but still harsh |
| **`combined`** | Blends `standard` + `basic` | Moderately softened |
| **`multidirectional`** | Simulates light from **four** azimuths (315°, 45°, 135°, 225°) and averages them | Very smooth, “puffy” relief, minimal hard shadows |
| **`igor`** | Experimental, mimics the *Igor* plugin in QGIS – a subtle, low‑contrast look | Good for background basemaps |

**Recommendation:** start with `"multidirectional"` – it gives a gentle, almost “ambient‑occlusion” feel with a single layer.

```json
{
  "id": "hillshade",
  "type": "hillshade",
  "source": "terrain",          // your raster‑dem source
  "paint": {
    "hillshade-method": "multidirectional"
  }
}
```

If you prefer a slightly less “fluffy” look, try `"combined"`.

---

## 2. Tweak the illumination direction (only for single‑light methods)

When you keep `hillshade-method: "standard"` (or `"basic"`), the sun azimuth strongly determines the visual harshness.

```json
"paint": {
  "hillshade-illumination-direction": 315,   // degrees clockwise from north
  "hillshade-illumination-anchor": "map"    // or "viewport"
}
```

* **Move the sun away from the map’s diagonal** – e.g. try **135°** (south‑east) or **45°** (north‑east).  
* **Set the anchor to `"viewport"`** if you want the sun to stay fixed on the screen while the map rotates (helps keep shadows consistent for user‑oriented navigation).

---

## 3. Reduce the contrast (exaggeration)

`hillshade-exaggeration` works like a gain control for the slope‑derived shading. The default is `1`. Lowering it softens both shadows and highlights.

```json
"paint": {
  "hillshade-exaggeration": 0.4   // 0‑1 = softer, >1 = harsher
}
```

Typical values for a gentle look are **0.3 – 0.6**.

---

## 4. Lighten the shadows and tone down the highlights

The built‑in colors are dark (`rgba(0,0,0,0.5)`) and bright (`rgba(255,255,255,0.5)`). Over a colored basemap they can dominate the visual hierarchy.

```json
"paint": {
  "hillshade-shadow-color":    "rgba(30,40,80,0.35)",   // cool‑blue, semi‑transparent
  "hillshade-highlight-color": "rgba(255,240,200,0.30)", // warm gold, very light
  "hillshade-accent-color":    "rgba(10,15,50,0.45)"    // optional deeper accent
}
```

* **Shadow color:** choose a cooler hue (blue‑purple) and lower opacity.  
* **Highlight color:** a warm, almost‑transparent gold keeps the terrain “lit” without washing out the basemap.  
* **Accent color:** only needed if you want a subtle ridge line effect.

---

## 5. Add a tiny amount of *ambient* light with a second hillshade (optional)

If you still want a little extra depth without the performance hit of a full multi‑pass stack, add a **second hillshade layer** that uses a different direction and a very low opacity.

```json
{
  "id": "hillshade‑soft‑extra",
  "type": "hillshade",
  "source": "terrain",
  "paint": {
    "hillshade-illumination-direction": 45,
    "hillshade-exaggeration": 0.2,
    "hillshade-shadow-color": "rgba(0,0,0,0.15)",
    "hillshade-highlight-color": "rgba(255,255,255,0.10)",
    "hillshade-accent-color": "rgba(0,0,0,0)"
  }
}
```

Place this **above** the main hillshade in the layer order, but **below** any vector or raster data you want to stay crisp. The extra pass adds a whisper of light from a different angle, making the terrain feel more three‑dimensional without the heavy cost of a true multi‑pass (four‑direction) algorithm.

---

## 6. Verify the DEM source & encoding

A harsh look can also be caused by **wrong elevation values** (e.g., inverted or flattened terrain). Make sure:

| Setting | Typical value for open sources |
|---------|--------------------------------|
| `type` | `"raster-dem"` |
| `encoding` | `"terrarium"` for AWS Terrain Tiles, Mapterhorn, etc. |
| `tileSize` | `512` (default for most terrain providers) |
| `url` | `pmtiles://terrain.pmtiles` or `https://.../{z}/{x}/{y}.png` |

```json
{
  "type": "raster-dem",
  "url": "pmtiles://terrain.pmtiles",
  "tileSize": 512,
  "encoding": "terrarium"
}
```

If the DEM is encoded as `"mapbox"` but you set `"terrarium"` (or vice‑versa), the elevation will be wildly off, which often results in a flat‑looking or overly‑contrasted hillshade.

---

## 7. Full example – a gentle hillshade ready to copy‑paste

```json
{
  "version": 8,
  "sources": {
    "terrain": {
      "type": "raster-dem",
      "url": "pmtiles://terrain.pmtiles",
      "tileSize": 512,
      "encoding": "terrarium"
    },
    "basemap": {
      "type": "raster",
      "tiles": ["https://.../sat/{z}/{x}/{y}.jpg"],
      "tileSize": 256
    }
  },
  "layers": [
    {
      "id": "basemap",
      "type": "raster",
      "source": "basemap"
    },
    {
      "id": "hillshade",
      "type": "hillshade",
      "source": "terrain",
      "paint": {
        "hillshade-method": "multidirectional",
        "hillshade-exaggeration": 0.45,
        "hillshade-shadow-color":    "rgba(30,40,80,0.30)",
        "hillshade-highlight-color": "rgba(255,240,200,0.25)",
        "hillshade-accent-color":    "rgba(10,15,50,0.40)"
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

*If you need the map to be **3‑D**, add the terrain mesh after the hillshade:*

```js
map.on('load', () => {
  map.setTerrain({source: 'terrain', exaggeration: 1.2});
});
```

The hillshade will stay in the background, softened by the multidirectional algorithm and the custom colors.

---

## 8. Performance checklist (so the soft hillshade stays fast)

| ✅ Check | Why it matters |
|--------|----------------|
| **One `raster-dem` source** shared by hillshade (and 3D terrain if used) | Avoids duplicate tile fetches |
| **`hillshade-method: "multidirectional"`** (instead of stacking 3–4 `hillshade` layers) | Single draw pass, lower GPU load |
| **Tile size 512** (most terrain providers) | Fewer tiles → less network overhead |
| **Exaggeration ≤ 1.5** on low‑end devices | Keeps the mesh small, reduces FPS drops |
| **Disable `terrain` on low‑power devices** (e.g., `if (navigator.hardwareConcurrency < 4)`) | Prevents severe FPS loss when the mesh is the bottleneck |

---

## 9. Quick‑fire “Harshness‑to‑Soft” checklist

| Step | Action |
|------|--------|
| 1️⃣ | Set `"hillshade-method": "multidirectional"` (or `"combined"`). |
| 2️⃣ | Lower `"hillshade-exaggeration"` to **0.4 – 0.6**. |
| 3️⃣ | Use semi‑transparent, cooler shadow (`rgba(30,40,80,0.3)`) and warm, light highlight (`rgba(255,240,200,0.25)`). |
| 4️⃣ | If you keep `"standard"`, change `"hillshade-illumination-direction"` away from the diagonal (try **135**). |
| 5️⃣ | Verify the DEM source `encoding` matches the tile provider. |
| 6️⃣ | Test on a low‑end device; if FPS drops, drop the extra hillshade layer or switch to `"basic"` method. |

---

### TL;DR

*Switch to `hillshade-method: "multidirectional"` (or `"combined"`), tone down the contrast with `hillshade-exaggeration` ≈ 0.4, give the shadows a cool, semi‑transparent color, and make sure your DEM source uses the correct `encoding`. The result is a smooth, natural‑looking hillshade that works nicely under any basemap without the harsh, cartoon‑ish look.*

Below is a short‑but‑complete recipe for getting **OSM‑derived roads + buildings** onto a MapLibre GL JS map.

---

## 1️⃣ Choose a vector‑tile provider

| Provider | URL pattern (no API key) | Free tier / limits | Why it works for roads + buildings |
|----------|--------------------------|-------------------|-----------------------------------|
| **OpenMapTiles (free “OpenMapTiles‑OSM” tileset)** | `https://free.tilehosting.com/data/v3.json?key=YOUR_KEY` | 100 000 tiles / day, no credit‑card required | The official OpenMapTiles schema ships the layers you need (`building`, `transportation`, `transportation_name`, …). |
| **MapTiler (free “basic” key)** | `https://api.maptiler.com/tiles/v3/tiles.json?key=YOUR_KEY` | 100 000 tiles / day, requires a free API key | Same OpenMapTiles schema, CDN‑optimised, HTTPS‑only. |
| **Protomaps “PMTiles” (self‑hosted)** | `pmtiles://my‑osm‑tiles.pmtiles` | Unlimited (you host it) | Great if you already have a PMTiles archive of the OpenMapTiles schema. |
| **Stadia Maps (raster only)** | `https://tiles.stadiamaps.com/tiles/osm/{z}/{x}/{y}.png` | 100 000 tiles / day | Raster tiles – you can still draw roads/buildings, but you lose the ability to style them client‑side. Use only if you *must* stay raster. |

> **Bottom line:** For full client‑side styling (the usual MapLibre workflow) pick a **vector‑tile source** that follows the OpenMapTiles schema – the two free hosted options above are the easiest to start with.

---

## 2️⃣ Add the source to your style JSON

```json
{
  "version": 8,
  "sources": {
    "osm": {
      "type": "vector",
      "url": "https://free.tilehosting.com/data/v3.json?key=YOUR_KEY",
      "maxzoom": 14,
      "attribution": "© OpenStreetMap contributors"
    }
  },
  "layers": [
    /* … your other layers (basemap, terrain, etc.) … */
  ]
}
```

*If you are using a PMTiles file instead of a remote URL, replace the `url` line with:*

```json
"url": "pmtiles://my-osm-tiles.pmtiles"
```

(You’ll need the **maplibre‑pmtiles** plugin to register the `pmtiles://` protocol – see the `maplibre-pmtiles-patterns` skill.)

---

## 3️⃣ Add the **building** layer

```json
{
  "id": "building",
  "type": "fill",
  "source": "osm",
  "source-layer": "building",          // <-- OpenMapTiles layer name
  "minzoom": 13,
  "paint": {
    "fill-color": "#d0c9c0",
    "fill-outline-color": "#a89f94",
    "fill-opacity": 0.7
  }
}
```

*Tips*

* `minzoom: 13` keeps the map fast – buildings are only drawn when you’re zoomed in enough to see them.
* Change the colour/opacity to match your basemap (e.g. a light‑gray fill works well over satellite imagery).

---

## 4️⃣ Add the **road** layers

OpenMapTiles splits roads into three source‑layers:

| source‑layer | what it contains |
|--------------|------------------|
| `transportation` | all road geometries (highways, primary, secondary, …) |
| `transportation_name` | road name labels (optional) |
| `transportation_z13` … `transportation_z15` | simplified versions for low zooms (optional) |

A minimal, good‑looking road stack looks like this:

```json
/* 1️⃣ Primary & secondary roads – thicker, coloured */
{
  "id": "road-major",
  "type": "line",
  "source": "osm",
  "source-layer": "transportation",
  "filter": ["in", "class", "motorway", "trunk", "primary", "secondary"],
  "layout": {
    "line-cap": "round",
    "line-join": "round"
  },
  "paint": {
    "line-color": [
      "match",
      ["get", "class"],
      "motorway", "#e84a5f",
      "trunk",    "#ff847c",
      "primary",  "#fecea8",
      "secondary","#99b898",
      "#cccccc"   // fallback
    ],
    "line-width": [
      "interpolate",
      ["linear"],
      ["zoom"],
      5, 0.5,
      12, 2,
      16, 6
    ]
  }
}

/* 2️⃣ Minor roads – thinner, lighter */
{
  "id": "road-minor",
  "type": "line",
  "source": "osm",
  "source-layer": "transportation",
  "filter": ["in", "class", "tertiary", "residential", "service", "unclassified", "road"],
  "layout": {
    "line-cap": "round",
    "line-join": "round"
  },
  "paint": {
    "line-color": "#ffffff",
    "line-width": [
      "interpolate",
      ["linear"],
      ["zoom"],
      5, 0.2,
      12, 1,
      16, 3
    ],
    "line-opacity": 0.8
  }
}

/* 3️⃣ Optional: road name labels */
{
  "id": "road-labels",
  "type": "symbol",
  "source": "osm",
  "source-layer": "transportation_name",
  "layout": {
    "text-field": ["get", "name"],
    "text-font": ["Open Sans Regular", "Arial Unicode MS Regular"],
    "text-size": [
      "interpolate",
      ["linear"],
      ["zoom"],
      12, 10,
      16, 14
    ],
    "text-offset": [0, 0.6],
    "text-anchor": "top"
  },
  "paint": {
    "text-color": "#222222",
    "text-halo-color": "#ffffff",
    "text-halo-width": 1
  }
}
```

*Why the filter?*  
OpenMapTiles stores the road “class” (motorway, primary, residential, …) as a string property called `class`. The filter lets you style each class differently without creating a separate layer for every class.

---
